claims.text: The initial HEA has a uniform single-phase BCC or FCC solid solution with homogeneous elemental distribution.
High mechanical loading causes microstructural evolution in an initially single-phase HEA.
Mechanical loading induces local atomic clustering or ordering, especially at grain boundaries.
Stress-induced clusters or ordered regions nucleate and promote the growth of brittle intermetallic precipitates or secondary phases.
Secondary phases introduced by processing can coexist with brittle tensile behavior in an HEA.
The secondary phases are themselves brittle and causally reduce toughness.
Brittle precipitates or ordered phases act as crack-initiation sites.
Local mechanical stresses drive atomic rearrangements in a metastable single-phase solid solution.
Those stress-driven rearrangements enhance short-range ordering or clustering and eventually cause precipitation.
HEAs can exhibit brittle fracture without detectable prior plastic deformation during room-temperature tension or elevated-temperature creep testing.
Relative to unloaded controls, mechanically preloaded specimens will have lower toughness, fracture strain, and ductility.
Relative to unloaded controls, mechanically loaded specimens will contain newly formed clusters or secondary phases at grain boundaries.
A nominally single-phase HEA can decompose into an ordered and disordered two-phase mixture as conditions change.
Composition and temperature can govern the occurrence and length scale of phase decomposition in an HEA.
Processing history can alter phase constitution in an HEA.
There are stress, strain-rate, and temperature thresholds above which mechanical loading initiates microstructural reordering.
The proposed behavior applies to high-cycle fatigue or high-stress aerospace service.
The baseline material has known toughness and ductility metrics while retaining its single-phase structure.
A lack of statistically significant toughness changes and a lack of new phases or clustering after cyclic loading would falsify the proposed stress-induced embrittlement mechanism.
